pedagogy.summary: Children learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, to make 3-D shapes from modelling materials (e.g. straws for edges and connectors for vertices), and to recognise a 3-D shape when it is rotated or seen from a different angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube needs 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence — children anchored to a canonical view judge a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. Best taught by handling and rotating real solids, and by building frames while counting edges and vertices.
bestPractices: Build 3-D frames from straws (edges) and connectors (vertices), counting how many of each are needed first (a cube: 12 edges, 8 vertices) and checking equal straw lengths so faces are square.
Let children physically rotate a solid — point-up, on its side, point-down, viewed from above — and re-name it each time, so the name is seen to be invariant to orientation.
Name solids by their properties (a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than by a single remembered picture, so rotation doesn't change the name.
Draw 2-D shapes on dotted paper/geoboards, marking each side as it is drawn to keep the count and closure accurate.
Connect nets and faces to the built solid, so each face is seen as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
keyRepresentations: Straws-and-connectors (or clay balls and sticks) for building edge/vertex frames
A real solid to grab and rotate through many orientations
Dotted paper / geoboard for accurate 2-D drawing
Nets that fold into the solid, linking 2-D faces to the 3-D shape
commonMisconceptions: Does not recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — calls a rotated or point-down pyramid 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or with the wrong number of sides.
Treats a shape's name as tied to its usual position, so turning it seems to change what it is.

learn.summary: Children (age 7-8) learn to draw 2-D shapes accurately, build 3-D solids from modelling materials, and recognise a 3-D shape as the same shape when it is rotated or seen from a new angle. Two procedural strands matter: constructing a solid correctly requires coordinating its edge/vertex/face structure (a cube has 12 equal edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces), and orientation recognition requires naming a shape by properties that stay the same under rotation. The central obstacle is orientation dependence: a child anchored to a canonical view judges a rotated or point-down solid to be 'a different shape'. The curriculum calls for making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so hands-on building, rotating real solids, and careful drawing on dotted paper/geoboards are the core activities; on-screen builders and spinners are useful complements, and recognition tasks can check outcomes but do not by themselves elicit construction.

activities.title: Build a cube frame from straws and connectors
feedback: If the frame has the wrong number of straws or connectors, re-establish the target first (12 edges, 8 vertices) and rebuild, counting each piece as it is added.

If the faces are not square, check that all straws are equal length and that the corners are right angles; unequal straws give a cuboid or an irregular frame rather than a cube, and even equal straws can lean into diamond-shaped faces unless the frame is squared up.
Compare the built frame side by side with a real cube-shaped solid to spot missing or extra edges.
activities.rationale: Properties of 3-D shapes are faces (flat 2-D surfaces), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where edges meet); handling real solids and marking each feature supports accurate counting and grounds the structure a child must coordinate when building a cube.
sourceClaims: Properties of 3-D shapes are the faces (flat 2-D surfaces), edges (straight lines where two faces meet) and vertices (corners where two or more edges meet); handling real solids and marking each feature supports accurate counting — grounds the edge/vertex/face structure a child must coordinate when building a cube.
learnerActions: Before building, predict and count how many edges (straws) and vertices (connectors) a cube needs, and state the target: 12 edges, 8 vertices, 6 square faces.
Build the cube frame, snapping straws (edges) onto connectors (balls of clay or plastic joints for vertices).

Check that every straw is the same length and that the corners are square (right angles, not leaning), because equal straws alone can still give a squashed frame with diamond-shaped faces; then compare the finished frame against a real cube-shaped solid.
Point to and count the edges, vertices and faces on the completed frame to confirm the structure.
Try building a cuboid with edges of different lengths as a contrast and describe how it differs from the cube (not all edges equal, so some faces are rectangles that are not squares).
activities.intendedInsight: A cube is defined by its structure — 12 equal edges, 8 vertices and 6 square faces — and building it requires coordinating that structure rather than approximating a box shape.

activities.title: Rotate a solid and keep naming it
feedback: If the child renames a point-down or sideways shape, hand them the same object and let them rotate it continuously so they see it never changed into something else.
Redirect naming to invariant properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) rather than to a remembered picture of its usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a hard case — linger there and ask the child to name the faces they can see and feel.
activities.rationale: Young children often treat orientation as a defining feature and may reject a rotated shape as not matching their prototype; rotated or non-standard triangles are commonly among the harder 2-D cases, and similar orientation dependence can affect 3-D solids such as a point-down pyramid. The suggested remedy is to present and handle shapes in varied orientations and to name by properties.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that children may not recognise a 2-D shape when it is presented in a different orientation; the remedy is to let children handle and rotate cut-outs to explore how a shape looks in different orientations, and to touch the sides and vertices as they count.

Young children treat orientation as a defining feature (e.g. rejecting a rotated shape), an 'imposed attribute' matching the prototype; a rotated isosceles triangle is the hardest case, with even a prototypical triangle missed by ~15% once rotated. Remedy: present shapes in varied orientations.
learnerActions: Hold a real pyramid (or cube) and physically turn it: point-up, on its side, point-down, and viewed from directly above.
At each orientation, say what the shape is and how you know, naming it by its properties (e.g. 'a pyramid has triangular faces meeting at an apex').
State explicitly whether the name changed when the shape turned, and explain why it should not.
Repeat with a cuboid laid on different faces, confirming it is the same solid each time.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's name comes from properties that do not change when it is rotated or viewed from a new angle; turning a solid does not make it a different shape.

activities.title: Draw 2-D shapes accurately on dotted paper or a geoboard
feedback: If the figure is not closed, return to the starting dot and count sides until the path closes.
If a side is curved, redraw it as a straight segment between two dots.
If there are too few or too many sides, re-count aloud while re-drawing, marking each side as it is placed.
activities.rationale: Marking each side as it is drawn and using dotted paper/geoboards supports accurate counting and closure; varying size while keeping the name reinforces that the name derives from invariant properties, not appearance. This strand follows the pedagogy's stated best practice; no cited source directly establishes its efficacy.
learnerActions: Draw named 2-D shapes (triangle, rectangle, pentagon, hexagon) on dotted paper or a geoboard.
Count and mark each side as it is drawn, keeping track so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
After drawing, re-count the sides and check the shape is closed and has straight (not curved) edges.
Draw the same shape again at a different size and confirm it keeps its name (a bigger hexagon is still a hexagon).
activities.intendedInsight: An accurate 2-D shape is a closed figure with the correct number of straight sides; its name depends on properties such as closure, side count and, for shapes like rectangles, right angles, not on size.

activities.title: Link nets and faces to the built solid
feedback: If the child cannot see a face as a 2-D shape, lay the net flat and trace one face, then fold it back into place on the solid.
Count the faces on both net and solid to confirm they match.
Note that a folded card net is a thin physical approximation of the ideal solid, which has zero-thickness faces — it stands in for the mathematical shape it represents.
activities.rationale: Connecting nets and faces to the built solid lets each face be seen as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model, reinforcing the face/edge/vertex structure. This activity extends the pedagogy's stated best practice; no source directly establishes its efficacy.
learnerActions: Fold a net into a solid, then identify each face as a 2-D shape within the 3-D model.
For a built cube frame, point out where each square face sits between four edges.
Match the faces on the net to the faces on the solid, naming the 2-D shape of each (square, triangle).
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a solid is a 2-D shape, so 2-D and 3-D shape knowledge connect: a cube's faces are squares, a pyramid's faces include triangles.

activities.title: On-screen builder and spinner (complementary digital practice)
feedback: If the digital frame will not close, use the tally to find which count is short and add or correct that feature.
After watching the point-down pyramid keep its name on screen, re-do the same rotation with a real wooden pyramid to confirm it feels the same.

A recognition choice (e.g. 'which picture is the same pyramid rotated?') can check whether orientation is understood, but follow it with an actual build or rotation task, since choosing does not show the child can construct or turn a solid themselves.
activities.rationale: Both hard parts are spatial — coordinating edge/vertex/face structure while building and seeing a shape as the same under rotation — and interactive builders with a live tally plus a grab-and-spin solid can make these visible. A flat projection only approximates free 3-D construction and rotation, so physical materials remain central; comparative efficacy is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Using a construction tool, snap virtual edges onto vertices to build a cube; watch a live tally of edges, vertices and faces update as you work.
Notice that a lopsided attempt with unequal edges does not resolve into a correct cube until the structure matches 12 edges, 8 vertices and six square faces.
Grab and spin an on-screen pyramid through point-up, on-its-side, point-down and top-down views, reading a label that continues to name it 'a pyramid' in every orientation.
Where possible, pair each on-screen task with the matching physical build or real solid so the hands confirm the screen.
activities.intendedInsight: A live edge/vertex/face tally and free rotation make the structure and its invariance under rotation visible; the digital model complements, and does not replace, handling real solids.

constraints: The curriculum requires making 3-D shapes from modelling materials, so children should build frames and turn real solids, not only watch or tap.

Recognition tasks (multiple-choice 'which is the same shape rotated?', or picking a drawn path) can check outcomes but do not let a child build a frame or freely rotate a solid, so they must not replace construction and manipulation.

On-screen builders and spinners are useful complements but approximate true 3-D construction and free rotation in a flat projection; pair them with real straws, clay/connectors and a wooden solid where possible.

Paper and card cut-outs and straw frames have real thickness; treat them as physical approximations of the ideal mathematical solid (whose faces have zero thickness), and treat any zero-thickness screen model as a model of the solid it represents.

Name shapes by invariant properties (for 2-D: closure, number of straight sides and, where relevant, angles such as a rectangle's right angles; for 3-D: faces/edges/vertices and how they meet), not by a single remembered picture or usual position.
The point-down pyramid is often a particularly demanding orientation case for recognition and deserves extra attention.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The dotted-paper/geoboard drawing activity and the nets activity derive from the pedagogy's stated best practices; no cited source directly establishes their efficacy, so both carry sourceClaims [].

In 'Rotate a solid and keep naming it', the Oak claim cited is about 2-D shapes in different orientations; it is applied here to 3-D solids by analogy. The orientation-invariance principle transfers and is independently supported by the EJMSTE finding, but no cited source tests this specifically for 3-D solids at this age.

The cited ~15% miss rate for a rotated prototypical triangle and the 'rotated isosceles triangle is hardest' finding come from a single study (Yeşil Dağlı & Halat, 2016) and are reported as claimed, not independently re-verified here.

The original recommendation leaned heavily on a specific 3D interactive and asserted a flat medium 'cannot' teach these spatial skills; that comparative/necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been softened to a complement with stated affordances and limits.

The original marked a static tap-to-reveal image and an in-role conversation as poor fits because they do not support active production; this is retained as the narrow observable point that recognition-only or role-play formats do not themselves elicit independent construction, without claiming they teach nothing.

The source claim about faces as 'flat 2-D surfaces' is strictly true for polyhedra like cubes and pyramids but not for curved solids; the activities here concern polyhedra, so the claim is applied appropriately.

probeDeeper: Turn the pyramid so it points downwards. Is it still a pyramid? How do you know?
Your cube frame — how many straws (edges) did you use? How many corners? Should a cube have that many?
Draw the same shape again but a different size. Is it still a hexagon?
I'll lay the cuboid down on a different face — is it a different shape now?
assess.correctAnswer: (1) A closed, six-sided, straight-edged figure. (2) A cube built from 12 equal straws (edges) and 8 connectors (vertices), giving 6 square faces. (3) Identifies it as the same pyramid in every orientation — a shape's name does not change when it is rotated or viewed from a different angle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to recognise a solid (or 2-D shape) in an unfamiliar orientation — says a rotated or point-down pyramid is 'a different shape' or 'not a pyramid'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Let them handle and physically rotate the solid so they see it is the same object throughout; name it by properties (triangular faces meeting at an apex) that do not change with orientation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When the pyramid is turned point-down or laid on its side, the child renames it or says it is no longer a pyramid.

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds the wrong frame — incorrect number of edges/vertices, or unequal edges so the faces are not square (a wonky frame or a cuboid when a cube was asked for).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish the target structure first — a cube needs 12 edges and 8 vertices — and check equal straw lengths for square faces, comparing the frame against a real cube.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The built frame has the wrong number of straws/connectors, or unequal straws so the faces are not square.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws 2-D shapes inaccurately — non-closed, curved-sided, or the wrong number of sides.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: draw on dotted paper/a geoboard, counting and marking each side as it is drawn so the figure closes with the right number of straight sides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The drawn hexagon is not closed, has a curved side, or has the wrong number of sides.

responseLevels.gap: Renames a shape when it is rotated or reoriented, builds a frame with the wrong edge/vertex structure, or draws non-closed/inaccurate figures.
responseLevels.full: Draws 2-D shapes accurately, constructs a cube/cuboid with the correct edges, vertices and faces, and recognises a solid as the same shape in ANY orientation — naming it by properties invariant to rotation and size (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Draws and builds correctly for familiar, canonical presentations and names a shape in its usual orientation, but falters when a solid is rotated to an unfamiliar view or when asked to reproduce an irregular/different-size version (SOLO multistructural).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set three tasks and watch: (1) 'Draw a hexagon as accurately as you can.' (2) 'Build a cube using these straws and connectors.' (3) Show a pyramid, then rotate it — lay it on its side, stand it point-down, show it from directly above — asking each time: 'Is this still the same shape? What is it?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The construction is a direct performance of edge/vertex/face structure: a child who holds the properties builds 12 edges and 8 vertices, while one who does not makes the wrong frame. The rotation task is the classic orientation probe — a child who names by properties keeps the name under rotation, while one anchored to a canonical view says the shape 'became different' when point-down. Watching the building and turning (not asking about them) shows which.
